# Episode 3: The Disruption Test
## "Is AI a Threat to the Business You're Buying?"

**Duration:** ~48 minutes
**Hosts:** Nadia & Owen
**Podcast:** The AI Diligence Room

---

### Cold open

[INTRO MUSIC]

**NADIA:** May 2023. The education company Chegg tells investors that student interest in ChatGPT is hurting its new customer growth. The shares fall by almost half in a day.

**OWEN:** February 2024. The payments company Klarna announces that its AI assistant is handling two thirds of its customer service chats in its first month, doing the equivalent work of seven hundred full-time agents.

**NADIA:** Two very different stories. In one, AI hits a company's revenue. In the other, AI hits a company's costs, and in this case, the revenue of whoever was providing those seven hundred agents.

**OWEN:** And for a private equity deal team, both stories ask the same question. If AI keeps getting better for the next five years, is the business we're about to buy going to be worth more, or less?

**NADIA:** Welcome back to The AI Diligence Room. I'm Nadia.

**OWEN:** I'm Owen. In the first two episodes, we looked at the target's own AI: whether its claims are true and what risks come with its technology. Today we flip it around. The disruption test. Whether AI threatens the target's business model, how to assess that in a few weeks of diligence, and how to turn the answer into a number.

**NADIA:** It's the hardest of the four questions, because it's about the future, and nobody knows the future. But it's also the one that can matter most to the price.

**OWEN:** Same notes as always. Public sources, made-up example companies, and not investment advice. Especially not investment advice today.

---

### Why this question got urgent

**NADIA:** Why is the disruption question so prominent right now?

**OWEN:** Because the market started pricing it in, fast. Bain's midyear private equity report this year described a triple shock, and the first part was an AI-driven selloff in software valuations. Investors began to worry that AI agents would reduce the number of people using seat-based software, that AI would let customers build things themselves, and that new AI-native competitors would undercut incumbents.

**NADIA:** And there were some sharp moves.

**OWEN:** Some very sharp ones. In early February, shares of several big legal and information services companies, including Thomson Reuters and RELX, fell steeply in a short period after Anthropic released industry-specific plugins for its Cowork agent product, including one aimed at legal work. Whatever you think of that reaction, it showed how quickly public investors will reprice a business when they see a credible AI substitute for part of what it sells.

**NADIA:** And private markets follow public markets.

**OWEN:** With a lag, and with less visible pricing, but yes. If comparable public companies are being repriced for AI risk, a buyer who ignores it is paying last year's multiple for this year's risk. And at exit, the next buyer will certainly ask. With holding periods of around seven years in Bain's data, the exit buyer will be looking at a world where AI has had a long time to do its work.

**NADIA:** So the disruption question is really about the exit.

**OWEN:** It's about the exit more than anything. The question isn't whether AI hurts the business next year. It's what the next buyer, five to seven years from now, will believe about the business's future. That's the horizon diligence has to think about.

---

### Who's exposed: a first map

**NADIA:** Let's start broad. Which kinds of businesses are most exposed?

**OWEN:** I'd group them by what the customer pays for. The most exposed are businesses where the customer pays for information or cognitive work that AI can now produce, and where the business doesn't control something hard to replicate. That includes some kinds of information services, some kinds of content, outsourced services like customer contact, translation and basic research, and software sold per user for tasks that AI agents can increasingly do.

**NADIA:** And the least exposed?

**OWEN:** Businesses where the value is physical, regulated, relationship-based or embedded in a system everyone depends on. A plumbing company. A lab with accredited testing. A distribution business with warehouses and trucks. A software system of record that holds a company's financial data and is deeply integrated into its processes. Those businesses can use AI to improve, and their competitors can too, but AI doesn't make them obsolete.

**NADIA:** And in the middle?

**OWEN:** The middle is where diligence earns its fee. Professional services, vertical software, data businesses with proprietary sources, marketing services, staffing, education. Parts of each are exposed, parts are protected, and the answer depends on the details of the specific company.

**NADIA:** So the map is a starting point, not an answer.

**OWEN:** Exactly. Two companies in the same sector can have very different exposure. A legal information company whose value is its editorial analysis, available elsewhere, is in a different position from one whose value is exclusive court data that nobody else has and that's integrated into lawyers' workflows.

---

### The task test

**NADIA:** How do you go from the map to a specific company?

**OWEN:** I use what I call the task test. Start with what customers actually pay for, and break it down into the tasks the product or service performs for them. Then ask, for each task, three questions: can AI do this task today, or soon, at acceptable quality? If so, who will capture that capability: the target, the customer, a competitor, or a big platform? And what's left that AI doesn't change?

**NADIA:** Give me an example.

**OWEN:** Take a made-up company. Meridian CX, a customer contact outsourcer. It provides customer service agents to retailers and utilities, mostly by phone and chat, billed per agent hour. What do customers pay for? Let's break it down. Answering simple questions, like order status or account balances. Handling transactions, like changing an address or processing a return. Solving complex problems, like billing disputes or technical faults. Handling upset or vulnerable customers. And the management of all of that: hiring, training, quality and reporting.

**NADIA:** And then the three questions.

**OWEN:** Can AI do it? Simple questions: largely yes, today. Transactions: increasingly yes, with the right system access. Complex problems: partly, with humans for the hard cases. Upset and vulnerable customers: mostly humans, for now. Management: changes in character, from managing people to managing a mix of AI and people.

**NADIA:** Who captures the capability?

**OWEN:** That's the critical question. For simple questions and transactions, the client could deploy AI itself, directly from a software vendor, and stop buying those agent hours from Meridian. Or Meridian could deploy AI for the client and charge for outcomes. Or a new AI-native outsourcer could win the work. So the business at risk is roughly the share of Meridian's hours that go to simple questions and transactions, and the question is whether Meridian keeps that business in a different form, or loses it.

**NADIA:** And what's left?

**OWEN:** The complex and human work, which may become more valuable per hour, and the expertise in running customer operations, which clients may still want to buy. The disruption doesn't take the business to zero. It changes its size and shape.

---

### Klarna and the human comeback

**NADIA:** Let's go back to Klarna, because the story has a second chapter.

**OWEN:** It does. In early 2024, Klarna's announcement was one of the most cited examples of AI replacing human work at scale. Then in 2025, Klarna's chief executive said publicly that the company would make sure customers could always reach a human, and Klarna started recruiting human customer service staff again, with the company acknowledging that focusing too much on cost had hurt quality.

**NADIA:** So the AI didn't work?

**OWEN:** I'd read it differently. The AI worked well for a large share of interactions, and Klarna kept using it. But the company learned, as many have, that the last part of customer service, the complex and emotional part, needs people, and that customers value knowing a human is available. The outcome wasn't zero humans. It was fewer, doing different work.

**NADIA:** And for the diligence team looking at an outsourcer like Meridian?

**OWEN:** It's a useful calibration. The disruption is real but partial. A model that assumes all simple contact goes to AI next year is too aggressive. A model that assumes nothing changes is too complacent. The right answer is a range, and the timing matters as much as the end state.

---

### How fast does it really move?

**NADIA:** You said the timing matters as much as the end state. How do you think about the pace?

**OWEN:** I separate three clocks. The technology clock, which is how fast AI capability improves. That's been very fast, with major model releases every few months and steady gains on real work tasks. The adoption clock, which is how fast businesses actually change how they work. That's much slower, because it needs integration, retraining, new processes, procurement, and trust. And the contract clock, which is how fast revenue actually moves, set by contract lengths and renewal dates.

**NADIA:** So even if the technology is ready today, the revenue might not move for years.

**OWEN:** For a business with three-year contracts, revenue at risk mostly moves at renewal. That buys time, and it also means the disruption, when it comes, comes in steps. A diligence team should map the renewal schedule against the exposure. If the most exposed customers all renew in the next eighteen months, the risk is near. If they're locked in for three years, there's time to act.

**NADIA:** And what speeds adoption up?

**OWEN:** Cost pressure, mostly. When customers are under pressure to cut costs, they adopt faster, and they look hardest at their outsourced services and software spend. Also competitive pressure, when a customer's own competitors adopt AI and gain an advantage. And easy adoption, when the AI capability comes built into tools the customer already uses, rather than requiring a new project.

**NADIA:** That last one is important.

**OWEN:** It's the big one. When a capability arrives as a feature in software that customers already have, like their office suite, their CRM or their ERP, adoption happens almost by default. That's why the big platforms are such a threat to point solutions. The customer doesn't have to make a decision to switch. The capability just shows up.

---

### Seats, outcomes and the pricing question

**NADIA:** Let's talk about software, because that's where the market reaction has been sharpest. What's the threat to software companies?

**OWEN:** There are three. The first is seat compression. A lot of business software is priced per user. If AI agents let a company do the same work with fewer people, it needs fewer seats. A customer service team that shrinks from a hundred agents to sixty buys sixty licenses, not a hundred. Even if the software becomes more valuable to the customer, the vendor's revenue falls unless the pricing changes.

**NADIA:** And the second?

**OWEN:** Substitution. AI makes it easier to build software. A customer that used to buy a niche tool might build a simple version itself with AI coding tools, or get the capability from a general-purpose AI assistant. That's more of a threat to simple, standalone tools than to complex systems.

**NADIA:** And the third?

**OWEN:** New competitors. AI-native startups, built from scratch around AI agents, that do the job differently. Instead of a tool that helps a person do a task, they sell the task done. Those companies often price by outcome or by usage rather than by seat.

**NADIA:** How are incumbents responding?

**OWEN:** Mostly by changing how they price and what they sell. Salesforce is the most visible example. When it launched its Agentforce product in 2024, it priced it at two dollars per conversation, rather than per seat, and in 2025 it added a credit-based model where customers pay per action the agent takes. Many software companies have moved toward hybrid pricing: a base subscription plus usage or outcomes for the AI.

**NADIA:** So for diligence, the pricing model is a key question.

**OWEN:** Maybe the key question for software targets. What share of revenue is priced per seat? In which customer segments are seat counts already falling, and why? Has the company introduced AI pricing, and what's the uptake? How do customers react to usage-based pricing? And what does the revenue look like in a scenario where seat counts drop by a quarter in the most exposed segments, offset partly by new AI revenue?

**NADIA:** Is seat compression already visible in the data?

**OWEN:** In some companies, yes, especially in customer service and some back-office categories. The best evidence in diligence is the company's own data: seat counts per customer over time, net revenue retention by segment, and the reasons customers give for reducing seats at renewal. If a customer reduced seats because its business shrank, that's normal. If it reduced seats because AI is doing the work, that's the trend you're worried about.

---

### Agents and the disappearing interface

**NADIA:** Let's talk about agents specifically, because a lot of the market's concern is about them.

**OWEN:** The worry is this. A lot of software value has been in the interface: the screens, the workflows, the reports that people use every day. That's where a vendor builds habit and loyalty. If AI agents do the work, and people just ask an agent for what they want, the interface matters much less. The agent might use several different systems behind the scenes, and the user might not even know which ones.

**NADIA:** So software becomes plumbing.

**OWEN:** Some of it, yes. And plumbing can be a good business, but it's priced differently. It's harder to charge per seat when no human sits in the seat. And it's easier to swap out, because the agent doesn't care about the interface, only about whether the system does its job reliably and cheaply.

**NADIA:** How does a diligence team test for that?

**OWEN:** Ask how much of the product's value is in the interface versus the data and the logic underneath. Ask whether the product is building ways for AI agents to use it, like interfaces designed for agents and connectors through open protocols. A vendor that makes itself easy for agents to use is positioning itself as essential plumbing. A vendor that resists, and tries to keep users in its own screens, may be fighting the tide.

**NADIA:** And is the vendor building its own agents?

**OWEN:** That's the other path, and many are. The best-positioned vendors have the data and the workflow, and they build agents that do the work inside their own systems, priced by outcome. That's often the strongest defense: be the agent, not just the system the agent uses.

---

### Systems of record and the moat question

**NADIA:** You said systems of record are more protected. Why?

**OWEN:** A system of record is where the authoritative data lives: the accounting system, the electronic health record, the field service management platform, the core banking system. Other systems, and now AI agents, need to read from it and write to it. That makes it the foundation the AI builds on, rather than something the AI replaces. And replacing a system of record is expensive and risky for the customer, so switching costs are high.

**NADIA:** But AI could still change them.

**OWEN:** It could change how people interact with them. If users talk to an AI agent instead of clicking through screens, the system of record's interface matters less. And that could weaken the vendor's relationship with the user, and its pricing power if it charges per user. But the data, the business logic, the integrations and the regulatory approvals remain valuable. In many cases, the system of record is in the best position to offer the AI agents itself, because it already has the data and the trust.

**NADIA:** So what makes a moat in an AI world?

**OWEN:** I'd list six. Proprietary data that's hard to get and keeps growing, like exclusive transaction data or data generated by the product's use. Deep workflow integration, where the product sits in the middle of how the customer works and is connected to everything else. Distribution: existing relationships with thousands of customers who trust you. Regulatory position: licenses, accreditations, approvals that take years to get. Physical assets and operations. And trust and accountability: customers who need someone to stand behind the work, legally and professionally.

**NADIA:** That last one is underrated.

**OWEN:** Very underrated. A lot of professional services, like audit, legal opinions, engineering sign-off, medical diagnosis, exist because someone has to be accountable. AI can do much of the underlying work, but the customer still needs a qualified person and a firm with insurance to stand behind it. That doesn't protect the hours billed, but it protects the relationship and the margin, if the firm adapts its pricing.

---

### Information services under pressure

**NADIA:** Let's take information services, since that's where some of the sharpest reactions were. How do you test a data or information business?

**OWEN:** Separate what's exclusive from what's assembled. Some information businesses own data nobody else has: proprietary surveys, transaction records, data contributed by members of a network, or exclusive licenses. Others assemble and organize information that's available elsewhere, and add analysis, curation and an interface. AI is very good at assembling, organizing, summarizing and analyzing. It can't create exclusive data out of nothing.

**NADIA:** So the exclusive data businesses are safer.

**OWEN:** Safer, and potentially more valuable, because AI companies and AI-using customers want high-quality data. Some data owners now license their content to AI companies, which is a new revenue stream. The assembled-information businesses are more exposed, especially if their main value is helping people find and summarize information, because that's exactly what AI assistants do.

**NADIA:** What about Chegg?

**OWEN:** Chegg is the textbook example, if you'll forgive the pun. Its core product helped students with homework questions and explanations. That's precisely what general-purpose chatbots do for free. Chegg's shares lost most of their value after 2023. In early 2025, Chegg sued Google, alleging that Google's AI summaries in search results were taking traffic and revenue from publishers like Chegg, and the company announced a strategic review. Whatever happens in that lawsuit, the lesson for diligence is clear: when your product does what a free AI assistant does, your pricing power disappears quickly.

**NADIA:** And the traffic issue more broadly?

**OWEN:** That's a threat to any business that depends on people finding it through search. If search engines answer questions directly with AI summaries, fewer people click through to websites. Publishers, comparison sites, review sites, and some lead-generation businesses have reported traffic declines. For a target that depends on search traffic, diligence should look at traffic trends by source over the last two years, and at how much of its traffic comes from informational searches that AI summaries could answer.

---

### Casebook: an information business

**NADIA:** Let's do a second made-up example, an information business. Call it Casebook. It sells a research platform to insurance claims teams: data on injury claims, settlement values and medical costs, plus analysis tools and summaries.

**OWEN:** Run the task test. What do customers pay for? Access to settlement and cost data. Search and analysis tools. Summaries and reports. And a reputation that lets claims teams justify their decisions to managers, regulators and courts.

**NADIA:** Where's the data from?

**OWEN:** That's the first big question. Say diligence finds that about half of Casebook's core data is contributed by its insurer customers under a data-sharing arrangement, which gives it a pooled view no single insurer has. The other half is assembled from public court records and published medical cost data, which anyone could gather with enough effort, and AI makes that effort much smaller.

**NADIA:** So half the data is exclusive.

**OWEN:** Half is genuinely exclusive and gets more valuable with each customer that contributes. That's a moat. The other half is assembled, and its value is shrinking, because AI can now gather and structure public records cheaply. A new competitor could build a reasonable version of that half in a year.

**NADIA:** And the tools and summaries?

**OWEN:** Highly exposed. Search, analysis and summaries are things general AI tools do well. Several customers in the diligence calls say they've started using AI assistants to analyze Casebook's data exports rather than using Casebook's own analysis tools. That's a warning, and also an insight. Customers still value the data. They're less attached to the tools.

**NADIA:** And the reputation?

**OWEN:** Strong. Claims teams say they cite Casebook in their files because it's accepted. A new competitor would need years to earn that.

**NADIA:** So what's the view?

**OWEN:** A business with a real moat in its contributed data and its reputation, and an exposed layer of tools and assembled data. The plan writes itself. Invest in the contributed data network, maybe extend it to more customers with better terms for contributors. Build AI capabilities on top of the exclusive data, so customers get answers grounded in data nobody else has, rather than generic analysis. Offer the data in forms that customers' own AI tools can use, priced appropriately. And accept that the analysis tools alone won't command the same price.

**NADIA:** And the price of the deal?

**OWEN:** It should reflect that some of today's revenue, from the tools and the assembled data, is at risk, and that the plan needs investment. But a buyer who sees the moat clearly might pay a fair price while others are scared off by the sector's general fear. That's where good diligence creates an edge.

---

### Services businesses: the hours problem

**NADIA:** And professional and business services? We touched on this in the Real Economy show.

**OWEN:** The core issue is the billing model. If a firm bills by the hour, and AI makes its people twice as fast at some tasks, then either it bills half the hours for that work, or it keeps the efficiency and moves to fixed fees. Customers increasingly know AI is speeding things up, and they push back on paying for hours they think AI did.

**NADIA:** How do you test that in diligence?

**OWEN:** Look at revenue by type of work and by pricing model. Which work is routine and AI-exposed, like document review, basic research, data entry, standard reports? Which is judgment-heavy and relationship-driven? What share of revenue is hourly versus fixed or value-based? Are clients already asking for AI-driven discounts? And is the firm using AI internally, so it can protect its margins as prices change?

**NADIA:** And the staffing model?

**OWEN:** Professional services firms traditionally have a pyramid: many junior people doing routine work, fewer senior people doing judgment work and client relationships. AI hits the base of the pyramid hardest. That can raise margins, if the firm needs fewer juniors for the same revenue. But it also raises a long-term question: if juniors don't do the routine work, how do they learn to become seniors? Firms that think about that will build a better talent pipeline than those that don't.

**NADIA:** And staffing firms?

**OWEN:** Staffing firms that place people in roles AI is changing face reduced demand in those roles, but they also have opportunities in new roles and in helping companies through the change. The diligence question is the mix of roles they place, and how exposed each is. A staffing firm focused on skilled trades and healthcare is in a very different position from one focused on data entry and basic administrative roles.

---

### Regulation: moat or drag?

**NADIA:** Where does regulation fit in the disruption test?

**OWEN:** It cuts both ways. For some businesses, regulation is a moat that slows AI disruption. If a task legally requires a licensed professional, an accredited lab or an approved device, an AI-native competitor can't simply replace the incumbent. It has to get the same approvals, which takes time and money. Healthcare, financial advice, audit, engineering sign-off and safety inspection all have elements of that.

**NADIA:** And the drag?

**OWEN:** Regulation can also slow the incumbent's own adoption of AI, while less regulated competitors move faster in adjacent areas. And new AI regulation can impose costs. A recruiting software company selling into Europe faces significant high-risk obligations under the EU AI Act by December 2027. A large incumbent can absorb that cost more easily than a startup, which might actually strengthen the incumbent's position. So in diligence, ask how regulation affects the target's AI plans and its competitors' AI plans, not just whether the target complies.

**NADIA:** And regulation can change.

**OWEN:** It can, in both directions, and quickly. A licensing requirement that protects a business today could be relaxed to allow AI services, or tightened. Treat regulatory moats as real but not permanent, and include a scenario where they weaken.

---

### Signals in the data room

**NADIA:** What can the diligence team look for in the data room that tells them disruption is already happening?

**OWEN:** Several signals. In software: seat counts falling per customer, especially at renewal, with AI cited as the reason. Net revenue retention dropping in specific segments. Pricing pressure in renewals. Customers asking about usage-based options. In services: clients asking for discounts tied to AI, or bringing work in-house, or moving work to AI-native providers. In information businesses: falling usage, falling traffic, customers questioning the value at renewal.

**NADIA:** And in the sales data?

**OWEN:** Win and loss data is a goldmine. Who is the company losing deals to? If AI-native competitors start appearing in the loss reasons, or customers say they chose to "build it with AI," that's an early signal. Look at the sales cycle too. If deals are taking longer because customers are waiting to see what AI can do, that's a sign of uncertainty in the market.

**NADIA:** What about the competitive landscape outside the data room?

**OWEN:** Look at funding. How much venture money has gone into AI-native competitors in the target's space in the last two years? Venture investors are effectively placing bets on which incumbents can be disrupted. If dozens of well-funded startups are attacking the target's core market, that's a signal, even if none of them is big yet. Then talk to a few of the target's customers about those startups. Have they tried them? What did they think?

**NADIA:** And management's view?

**OWEN:** Ask management directly: which parts of your business would you attack if you were an AI-native startup? A thoughtful management team will have a clear answer, and a plan. A defensive one will tell you there's no threat. The second answer is itself a risk factor.

---

### Questions for management on disruption

**NADIA:** Give me the short list of questions a deal partner should ask management on this topic.

**OWEN:** Eight questions. One: which parts of our revenue would an AI-native startup attack first, and why haven't they yet? Two: which customers have reduced spend in the last year, and what did they say about AI? Three: what share of revenue is priced per seat or per hour, and what's the plan for pricing?

**NADIA:** Four.

**OWEN:** Four: which large platforms could add what we do as a feature, and what would we do if they did? Five: what do we have that an AI system can't easily replicate: data, relationships, approvals, operations? Six: what are we doing with AI to make our own product or service better and cheaper?

**NADIA:** Seven and eight.

**OWEN:** Seven: if revenue in our most exposed segment fell by a quarter over three years, what would we do with the cost base? And eight: what would have to be true for us to be stronger in five years because of AI, not weaker? A good management team will have thought about all of these, and their answers will be specific. Vague answers are a finding.

---

### Customer research for the disruption question

**NADIA:** You mentioned customers. How do you design the customer research for this question?

**OWEN:** It's different from a normal satisfaction survey. You want to understand how customers are thinking about AI in their own operations, and how that affects what they'll buy from the target. So the questions are about the customer's plans as much as the target's product.

**NADIA:** Give me some.

**OWEN:** How are you using AI today in the work this product or service supports? What do you plan to do in the next two years? If AI could do part of what you buy from this company, would you rather the company provide it, buy it from someone else, or do it yourselves? Would you pay more, the same, or less for an AI-enhanced version of the service? How do you feel about paying by outcome rather than by user or by hour? And what would make you switch to a different provider?

**NADIA:** And who do you ask?

**OWEN:** A mix. The users of the product, because they know how it fits the work. The buyers, because they hold the budget and they're the ones under pressure to cut costs with AI. And for big customers, the people responsible for AI strategy, who often have a plan that the users don't know about yet. The gap between what users say and what the AI strategy team says is often where the risk is.

**NADIA:** How many conversations?

**OWEN:** For a mid-sized target, twenty to thirty customer conversations, plus a survey if the customer base is large, plus a few experts who know the market. That's enough to see patterns, especially if you deliberately include customers who've reduced their spend recently.

---

### Turning it into a number

**NADIA:** At some point, the deal team needs a number. How do you put the disruption question into the financial model?

**OWEN:** Scenarios, built from the task test. For each part of the revenue, estimate how much is exposed, when the pressure might start, how fast it could move, and how much the company could keep through new pricing or AI products. Then build three or four scenarios over the holding period, and through to the exit.

**NADIA:** Walk me through it for Meridian, our contact outsourcer.

**OWEN:** Say forty percent of Meridian's hours go to simple questions and transactions. In a base case, half of that work moves to AI over five years, starting slowly and accelerating. Meridian keeps some of it by offering AI-based services at lower prices but higher margins, and loses some to clients who do it themselves. Complex work grows a little. Net, revenue is roughly flat over five years, margins improve, and the business ends up with a different mix.

**NADIA:** And the bear case?

**OWEN:** In the bear case, most of the simple work moves to AI within three years, Meridian keeps very little of it, prices for complex work fall as competitors chase the remaining volume, and revenue declines by a third. Margins fall because fixed costs, like facilities, don't shrink as fast. That's a business you might still buy, but at a much lower price.

**NADIA:** And the bull case?

**OWEN:** In the bull case, Meridian moves quickly, becomes the trusted provider of AI-plus-human customer service for its clients, wins share from slower competitors, and grows revenue modestly with much higher margins. That's a much better business at exit than it is today.

**NADIA:** And how do you weight them?

**OWEN:** That's judgment, informed by the evidence. The customer research, the signals in the data, management's capability and plan, and the pace at which the technology is improving. And then the price has to work in the scenarios you think are plausible, not just the base case. If the deal only works in the bull case, you're paying for a transformation that hasn't happened yet.

**NADIA:** What about the exit multiple?

**OWEN:** That's where disruption bites hardest. Even if the earnings hold up, the exit buyer will apply a multiple that reflects its view of AI risk at that time. A business that looks exposed in five years will trade at a discount, regardless of current earnings. So the model should include a sensitivity on the exit multiple based on how the business is likely to be perceived. The best protection is to make the business clearly less exposed by the time you sell.

---

### From threat to plan

**NADIA:** So if the disruption test shows real risk, does the deal die?

**OWEN:** Not necessarily. Sometimes the right answer is to walk away. But often the risk is also the opportunity. A business with strong customer relationships, good data and a credible management team that's exposed to AI disruption can become the one doing the disrupting, with the right investment. That's a classic private equity thesis: buy a good business at a fair price because the market fears a change, and lead the business through it.

**NADIA:** What has to be true for that to work?

**OWEN:** Four things. A management team that sees the threat clearly and has the will to change, or that you're prepared to change. Enough customer trust and relationships that customers will buy the new version from the company, rather than going elsewhere. Enough financial room to fund the transition, including possibly lower revenue for a period. And a plan with milestones, so you know early whether it's working.

**NADIA:** What does the plan look like for Meridian?

**OWEN:** Launch AI-based contact services quickly, for the clients most likely to adopt them, priced by resolution or outcome. Retrain agents for complex work, quality management and AI supervision. Reduce facilities and fixed costs as volume shifts. Renegotiate contracts from per-hour to outcome-based pricing at renewal. Build a capability in designing and running AI customer service that clients will pay for. And track the share of revenue from new services, the margin on them, and client retention, every quarter.

**NADIA:** That's essentially reinventing the company.

**OWEN:** In a way, yes. And that's what the price needs to reflect: the cost and risk of that reinvention, and the value if it succeeds.

---

### Businesses AI makes stronger

**NADIA:** We've spent a lot of time on threats. Let's balance it. Which businesses does AI make stronger?

**OWEN:** More than people think. First, businesses with lots of skilled people doing a lot of paperwork, where AI takes the paperwork and the people do more of the skilled work. That's much of the real economy: healthcare services, field services, engineering, inspection. Second, businesses with proprietary data that becomes more valuable when AI can analyze it. Third, systems of record that become the foundation for AI agents. Fourth, businesses with strong distribution that can sell AI-powered products to an existing customer base quickly.

**NADIA:** And businesses that benefit from the AI boom directly?

**OWEN:** Yes, there's a whole category: data centers, power, cooling, electrical equipment, specialized construction and services for the infrastructure that AI needs. Many private equity funds have invested heavily there. Those have their own diligence questions about demand durability, but that's a different episode.

**NADIA:** And for the businesses AI makes stronger, what's the diligence question?

**OWEN:** Whether the company will capture the benefit, or whether its competitors will capture it just as well, so the benefit goes to customers in lower prices. If every HVAC company gets the same AI phone agent, the advantage disappears over time, and the benefit goes to customers. The companies that keep the advantage are those that execute better, faster and more consistently. So the question becomes about management capability and the operating model.

---

### Common mistakes

**NADIA:** What mistakes do deal teams make on the disruption question?

**OWEN:** Five common ones. First, treating it as a technology question and handing it to the technical advisor. It's a commercial and strategic question, and it needs commercial diligence. Second, asking only management, which will usually be optimistic. Third, extrapolating from today's AI capability, when the technology is improving fast. A task AI can't do well today may be routine in two years.

**NADIA:** Fourth.

**OWEN:** The opposite mistake: assuming disruption is immediate and total. Real adoption by businesses is slower than the technology's progress, because of integration, trust, regulation and inertia. Klarna-style announcements get headlines. Most businesses move gradually. Fifth, ignoring the exit. A deal team can convince itself that the business will be fine for five years, without asking how the business will look to a buyer at the end of those five years.

**NADIA:** And the best practice?

**OWEN:** Do the task test, talk to customers about their AI plans, look for signals in the data, build honest scenarios, and price the deal to work in the plausible ones. And if you buy an exposed business, have a plan from day one to make it less exposed by the time you sell.

---

### Takeaways

**NADIA:** Sum it up.

**OWEN:** The disruption question is about the exit, five to seven years out, as much as the next year. Start with a map of exposure, then do the task test: break down what customers pay for, ask whether AI can do each task, who will capture the capability, and what's left.

**NADIA:** For software?

**OWEN:** Check the pricing model. Seat-based revenue is exposed to seat compression. Look at seat counts, net retention by segment and the company's move to usage or outcome pricing.

**NADIA:** For information and services?

**OWEN:** Separate exclusive data from assembled information. For services, look at the billing model and the pyramid. Look for signals in win-loss data, renewals, traffic and competitor funding. Design customer research around customers' own AI plans.

**NADIA:** And the number?

**OWEN:** Build scenarios from the task test, include an exit multiple sensitivity, and make sure the price works in the plausible scenarios, not just the best one. And if the business is exposed but strong, the threat can be the thesis: buy it, lead the change, and sell a business that's less exposed than the one you bought.

**NADIA:** Next time, our last episode of the season: turning all of these findings into price, contract terms, insurance, and a plan for the first hundred days.

**OWEN:** Thanks for joining us in The AI Diligence Room. I'm Owen.

**NADIA:** And I'm Nadia. See you next time.
